JUDY GRACI’S BRIEF ON REMANDED PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13, OPPOSING APPROVAL OF THE APPLICATIONS

TO THE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Judy Graci, Pro se intervenor, in the above-captioned, consolidated proceedings, respectfully files this brief, as directed by SOAH Order No. 35, on the two issues that Chairman Gleeson's September 9, 2026, memorandum remanded to the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) for further findings. Those issues are Issue 11 (Reliability Necessity) and Issue 13 (Congestion Cost Savings). Ms. Graci opposes approval of both Applications. For the reasons below, she submits that the existing record cannot support affirmative findings on either remanded issue, that the Commission's rules are responsible for that evidentiary gap, and that the appropriate remedy is denial of the Applications. The two Applications seek certificates for the two halves of Import Path 2: the eastern half from Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation (Docket No. 59475) and the western half from Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch (Docket No. 59182). The issue of need for Import Path 2 was consolidated in this proceeding. This brief refers to the two together as “Import Path 2” or “the Project.”

I. SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Commission cannot simultaneously (a) have treated these projects as reliability projects exempt from the economic tests, including the congestion-cost-savings showing, and (b) now demand on remand that the ALJs manufacture a congestion-cost-savings finding (Issue 13) from a record that was never built to support one.
The ALJs' Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) already found the Applicants failed to establish sufficient generation at Bell County East to justify the westward power flow.  Applicants stated that neither Oncor nor ERCOT had studied Central Texas net generation under the relevant scenarios, had determined whether Central Texas generation could serve local data-center load while simultaneously exporting westward at Import Path 2’s design capacity, or had performed the corresponding sensitivity analysis.  Ms. Graci’s evidence that new and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2 altogether. That finding undercuts the factual predicate for treating these Applications as reliability projects, the classification that triggered the exemption from the economic tests (Issue 11).
Issue 11. Applicants’ evidence shows a forecast need for more transfer capacity. It does not show that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet an identified state or federal reliability standard. Applicants’ own witness acknowledged that no study isolated Import Path 2 from the other import paths, and Applicants have not shown that the claimed violations persist once approved local projects and available alternatives are accounted for. The PFD’s own findings on local generation point the same way.
Issue 13. The record contains no estimate of consumer congestion cost savings attributable to Import Path 2. It contains plan-level, statewide modeling, historical statewide congestion totals, and general testimony.

II. ISSUE 11 ---THE ALJS SHOULD BE DIRECTED TO IDENTIFY THE SPECIFIC NERC AND STATE RELIABILITY STANDARDS AT ISSUE, AND THE APPLICANTS BEAR THE BURDEN OF PROVING NON-COMPLIANCE WITHOUT THE PROJECT
Chairman Gleeson correctly observes that the PFD answered a different question than the one Issue 11 asked. Finding that the Project “will import power … into the Permian Basin” describes what the facilities do; it says nothing about whether the facilities are necessary to satisfy a specific, identifiable reliability standard. On remand, Ms. Graci urges the ALJs to require the Applicants — who bear the burden of proof under PURA §37.056 — to answer the following from the existing record:
Identify by name and number the specific NERC Reliability Standards (e.g., the TPL series for transmission planning, FAC series for facility ratings, or any applicable ERCOT Nodal Protocol requirement) that the Project is purportedly necessary to satisfy;
Point to prior evidence that identifies what specific standard would be violated — and under what load, generation, and contingency assumptions — if the Project is not built;
Address whether the compliance risk the Applicants identify could be resolved by non-transmission alternatives, including the new and planned Permian Basin gas generation that the ALJs already found the Applicants failed to adequately account for in the PFD; and
If the Applicants contend that a NERC standard violation would violate federal law, brief that legal question separately and specifically — including which federal statute or FERC-approved standard would be implicated, and what enforcement consequence would follow.
A generalized assertion that more transmission capacity would help reliability is not a finding that the capacity is necessary to meet an identified standard. Ms. Graci submits that if the Applicants cannot make this showing from the existing record on remand, that failure is independently sufficient grounds for denial — it is not a technicality to be cured by supplemental briefing that simply restates the need case in different languages.

A.  The evidence shows a forecast need for capacity, not the necessity of Import Path 2.
The PBRP study found that “multiple import paths” would be needed to serve projected load. A finding about a set of import paths is not a finding about Import Path 2. On cross-examination Mr. Gurley said he was “not aware” of a study that isolated each line independently, that the lines “were studied together,” and that he “assume[d]” this explained the recommendation for multiple lines. An assumption by the witness is not a showing of necessity.

The PFD has already made findings on this point. It found that Applicants performed no partial-build study to justify Import Path 2 individually, did not establish need for Import Path 2 separate from the three-path project, and that NERC contingencies shaping regional planning “are not a substitute for proving project-specific need.” It likewise found that the evidence did not establish that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030. The supplemental PFD on Issue 11 should be consistent with those findings.

The forecast that drives the claimed violations is also in doubt on this record. The PFD found that 61% of the PBRP’s non-oil-and-gas load rests on officer letters or is unconfirmed, that Mr. Gurley “would not say” those loads were verified, and that applying ERCOT’s own 2025 realization-rate methodology would cut the forecast by at least 3,571 MW, against an Import Path 2 safe loading limit of 5,270 MW. Staff’s witness agreed on cross-examination by Ms. Graci that the methodology behind this load forecast needs to change. Applicants’ studies did not test whether the claimed violations survive a corrected forecast.

B.  The PFD found that the Far West Import GTCs do not establish necessity.
The PFD found that the Far West Import GTCs have not resulted in any load shed to date; that GTCs measure transmission constraints and “do not validate the composition or reliability of the load” behind them; that Applicants do not separate the load driving the GTCs from the speculative load that undermines the PBRP forecast; and that the GTCs do not validate the PBRP’s load forecast or the necessity of Import Path 2. It also noted that ERCOT’s April 2026 presentation lists the 765-kV paths as one of seven upgrades that “help” exit the GTCs, not as the required fix.

C.  Local Permian Basin transmission has already been approved.
The Commission adopted the PBRP, including its common local projects, on October 7, 2024. ERCOT and the PUC have approved about $4.7 billion in local transmission upgrades in the Permian. Mr. Gurley testified that ERCOT updated the topology to include “planned” transmission.

D.  The PFD found that ERCOT’s recommendation should not receive great weight.
The PFD found that ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation relies on a forecast ERCOT’s own 2025 methodology would materially reduce, is not “substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth,” and should not be given great weight under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). It further found that even with great weight, the greater weight of credible evidence is against the recommendation.

III. ISSUE 13 — THE COMMISSION CANNOT DEMAND A CONGESTION-COST-SAVINGS FINDING FROM A RECORD ITS OWN RULE EXEMPTED THE APPLICANTS FROM BUILDING
PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) call for a cost-benefit analysis of economic projects, including the estimated cost to consumers and congestion cost savings. Applicants contend that reliability projects under § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii) are exempt from those economic tests, and the PFD agrees that the analysis was not required.

These Applications proceeded as reliability projects under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii). As a direct consequence, the evidentiary record was never built to support a congestion-cost-savings finding — no party was required to sponsor testimony quantifying current or forecasted redispatch costs, avoided congestion, or the counterfactual cost of not building the Project. Chairman Gleeson's memorandum now asks the ALJs to answer Issue 13 anyway. Ms. Graci submits that:
The absence of record evidence on congestion cost savings is not a gap the ALJs can fill by inference or by crediting the Applicants' general need testimony — it is the direct and foreseeable result of the exemption the Commission itself granted. If the existing record cannot answer Issue 13, the honest finding is that it cannot be answered, not a finding of savings unsupported by evidence.

The PFD found that the analysis of cost to consumers and congestion cost savings was not required for this reliability project, and that the record contains no evidence quantifying either. 
The Commission’s Project No. 55718 orders also exempted the PBRP projects from further ERCOT Regional Planning Group review, where alternatives would otherwise be submitted, and the PFD notes that Applicants were exempted from any alternatives analysis. The exemption does not reach necessity. HB 5066 does not make a project’s inclusion in a reliability plan a finding that it is needed, and need must be independently determined under PURA § 37.056.

A.  The modeling is plan-level and cannot isolate Import Path 2.
Issue 13 asks about savings that “may result from the proposed transmission facilities.” Applicants’ economic evidence compares whole statewide plans. The compared 765-kV plan is described as including the Permian Basin import paths and local projects. The 2025 RTP economic cases began with the STEP incorporated. Because Import Path 2 was assumed built in the starting case, the modeling cannot measure what it adds. And Mr. Gurley acknowledged that no study isolated Import Path 2 from the other import paths.

B.  The modeled savings depend on a load forecast the PFD found overstated.
The modeled figures also depend on the same load forecast the PFD found to be overstated. JG-4 begins from a forecast of more than 150 GW of 2030 summer peak demand, about 50 GW of it large load. The PFD found that the Commission ordered ERCOT in 2025 to discount officer-letter and data-center load because actual loads were “coming into service at lower megawatt levels than initially claimed,” producing a system-wide forecast demand reduction of about 27% for 2031 in ERCOT’s 2025 RTP. Savings modeled from a forecast later cut by that margin cannot be taken at face value, and Applicants did not rerun them.

IV. THE PFD'S EXISTING FINDINGS ON GENERATION ADEQUACY ALREADY UNDERMINE THE “RELIABILITY PROJECT” PREMISE
The ALJs' PFD found that the Applicants did not establish that Bell County East has sufficient generation to justify the Project's westward power flow, and credited Ms. Graci’s evidence that new and planned generation in the Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2. 

V. THE NOTICE VIOLATIONS FOUND IN THE PFD REMAIN AN INDEPENDENT AND SUFFICIENT BASIS FOR DENIAL
Nothing in the September 9 remand memorandum disturbs the ALJs' findings that the Applicants failed to comply with 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4)'s public-meeting notice requirements as to approximately 1,400 landowners whose properties were brought into the study area after the Applicants' 2025 public meetings, and who were never given the opportunity to provide community-value input on the routes ultimately filed. Ms. Graci reiterates that this due-process failure is, standing on sufficient grounds for denial under the ALJs' own PFD, and should not be displaced or diluted by the Commission's separate inquiry into Issues 11 and 13.

VI. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF
For the foregoing reasons, Ms. Graci respectfully requests that the ALJs, on remand:
Find, that Applicants have not shown Import Path 2 is necessary to meet an identified state or federal reliability standard (Issue 11), because no study isolates Import Path 2, the PFD found no project-specific need, and the claimed violations rest on an overstated load forecast;
Find, the existing record does not support a congestion-cost-savings determination under Issue 13, and that the record is insufficient to make that finding;


Reaffirm the PFD's independent finding that the notice violations affecting approximately 1,400 landowners warrant denial; and
Recommend that the Commission deny both Applications.

Respectfully submitted,

By:          /s/ Judy Graci	  

Judy Graci, Pro se Intervenor
1301 County Road 282
Bertram, Texas 78605
Telephone: (512) 422-5404
judithgraci@yahoo.com

in the starting case, the modeling cannot measure what it adds. And Mr. Gurley acknowledged

that no study isolated Import Path 2 from the other import paths.34




B. The modeled savings depend on a load forecast the PFD found overstated.

The modeled figures also depend on the same load forecast the PFD found to be overstated. JG-4

begins from a forecast of more than 150 GW of 2030 summer peak demand, about 50 GW of it

large load.35 The PFD found that the Commission ordered ERCOT in 2025 to discount officer-

letter and data-center load because actual loads were "coming into service at lower megawatt

levels than initially claimed," producing a system-wide forecast demand reduction of about 27%

for 2031 in ERCOT's 2025 RTP.36 Savings modeled from a forecast later cut by that margin

cannot be taken at face value, and Applicants did not rerun them.



IV. THE PFD'S EXISTING FINDINGS ON GENERATION ADEOUACY ALREADY

UNDERMINE THE "RELIABILITY PROJECT" PREMISE

The ALJs' PFD found that the Applicants did not establish that Bell County East has sufficient

generation to justify the Project's westward power flow, and credited Ms. Graci's evidence that

new and planned generation in the Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for Import

Path 2.37
